lesson.body:
Body is just the weight and texture of a wine in your mouth — how light or heavy it feels as you sip. The easiest way to picture it: imagine three glasses, one with skim milk, one with whole milk, and one with cream. They're all "milk," but each feels thinner or richer on your tongue. Wine works the same way, from light-bodied to full-bodied.

Two things mostly drive how full a wine feels: alcohol and "extract" — extract just means all the flavor and substance pulled from the grapes. More of either generally means more weight. (In sweet wines, leftover sugar adds richness too, but most everyday dry wines have almost none, so it's not the reason a dry red feels full.) To feel it yourself, take a sip and notice whether it seems watery and quick, or thick and lingering, almost coating your mouth.

Want examples? On the light side, try a Pinot Grigio or a basic Beaujolais — crisp and easygoing. On the full side, a Cabernet Sauvignon or an oaked Chardonnay feels bigger, rounder, and stays with you longer. Neither is better; it's just your preference.
outcomes: Explain what body means in a wine
Name the two main things that add body
Tell light-bodied from full-bodied wines by feel

deep_notes: Wine schools usually describe body on a simple scale of light, medium and full, with whole milk in the middle as medium. Body is one part of a wider idea tasters call mouthfeel: every texture a wine has, such as silky, creamy or grippy. Two wines can share the same body yet feel quite different, so it pays to notice both how heavy a wine is and how smooth it feels.

Alcohol makes wine slightly more viscous than water, meaning thicker and slower to flow, and it adds a gentle warmth. That is why a wine at 14.5% usually feels fuller than one at 11.5%. Extract covers what would be left if you boiled off the water and alcohol: things like acids, tannin (the drying grip many reds have), colour pigments and minerals. Riper grapes from warm places tend to give more of both alcohol and extract.

Body is easiest to judge by comparison. Water makes a handy baseline: sip some, then sip the wine, and notice how much more weight the wine has. Tasting two wines side by side helps even more. High alcohol often shows as a gentle warmth at the back of your throat, a hint that the wine will feel fuller. Remember that body and sweetness are separate: a completely dry wine can still feel rich.

Basic Beaujolais is made from Gamay, a grape that gives juicy reds low in tannin, the drying grip many reds have. It is often served lightly chilled. Pinot Grigio is the Italian name for Pinot Gris. In Italy it is usually picked early for a light, crisp style, while in Alsace the same grape often makes much fuller wines. Between the two ends sit medium-bodied wines, such as a typical Chianti.

deeper.body: Grape variety is only part of the story. Chardonnay from Chablis, in cool northern Burgundy, is usually lean and light to medium in body. Chardonnay from sunny California is often rich and full. More sun gives riper grapes with more sugar, the yeast turns that sugar into more alcohol, and more alcohol means more weight.
deeper.title: Same grape, different weight

deeper.why: Sun ripens grapes and builds sugar. More sugar becomes more alcohol, and more alcohol means a fuller body.

deeper.body: After fermentation, dead yeast cells called lees settle at the bottom of the tank or barrel. Leaving a wine on them for months, and sometimes stirring them up, a step called bâtonnage, gives a rounder, creamier texture. Time in oak barrels can round a wine out too. Together they help explain why an oaked Chardonnay feels so much bigger than a crisp, unoaked white.
deeper.title: Lees and oak add cream

deeper.q: Winemakers stir the lees to make a wine feel leaner and lighter.
deeper.why: Stirring the lees does the opposite: it gives the wine a rounder, creamier, fuller texture.

deeper.body: Body is one of the most useful clues when pairing wine with food. A light wine suits delicate dishes, like a leafy salad or white fish. A full wine stands up to rich ones, like a beef stew. Get it wrong and one side wins: a big red can swamp a delicate dish, and a light wine can taste thin and watery next to heavy food.
deeper.title: Match weight with weight

v2.body:
Swirl a glass of wine and you may see clear drops form near the rim and run back down the inside. They are called **tears**, or legs. In 1855 the scientist James Thomson, elder brother of Lord Kelvin, explained them: alcohol evaporates (turns to vapour) faster than water, and that pulls a thin film of wine up the glass. More alcohol usually means more tears. They say nothing about quality, but they are a first clue to this lesson's idea.

**Body** is the weight and texture of a wine in your mouth: how light or heavy it feels as you sip. Picture three glasses: skim milk, whole milk and cream. All are milk, yet each feels thinner or richer on your tongue. Wine works the same way, from **light-bodied** through medium to **full-bodied**, with whole milk as the middle. Body is a feeling, so two wines of the same colour can have very different bodies.

Two things mostly drive how full a wine feels: alcohol and **extract**. Alcohol makes wine slightly thicker than water and adds a gentle warmth, so a wine at 14.5% usually feels fuller than one at 11.5%. Extract means all the flavour and substance from the grapes: what would be left if you could take away the water and the alcohol, such as acids (sourness), colour and tannin (the drying feel of strong tea). More of either generally means more weight. In sweet wines, leftover sugar adds richness too, but most everyday dry wines have almost none, so sugar is not why a dry red feels full.

Where the grapes grow matters. Sun ripens grapes and builds sugar, and yeast, the tiny living things that make wine, turns more sugar into more alcohol. So the same grape can make a lighter wine in a cool place and a fuller one in a warm place. Chardonnay from Chablis, in cool northern Burgundy in France, is usually light, while Chardonnay from sunny California is often rich and full.

To feel body, take a sip and focus on the texture, not the flavour. Does the wine seem watery and quick? Or thick and lingering, almost coating your mouth? The first is light-bodied, the second full-bodied. A sip of water first gives you a handy baseline.

Want examples? On the light side, try a Pinot Grigio (an Italian white) or a basic Beaujolais (a French red): crisp and easygoing. A typical Chianti, an Italian red, sits in the middle. On the full side, a Cabernet Sauvignon or an **oaked Chardonnay** (aged in oak barrels) feels bigger, rounder and stays with you longer. Neither is better. Body is a matter of taste, so pick the style you enjoy.
deep_notes: Tears go by many names: legs, fingers, curtains, and in German Kirchenfenster, church windows. They show best in strong wines, and a poor wine can have plenty of them if its alcohol is high enough. So treat them as a hint about alcohol, and so about weight, never as a score. The 1855 scientist was James Thomson. The effect is now named after the Italian physicist Carlo Marangoni, who published his own work on it ten years later.

Wine schools usually describe body on a simple scale of light, medium and full, with whole milk in the middle as medium. Body is one part of a wider idea tasters call mouthfeel: every texture a wine has, such as silky, creamy or drying. Two wines can share the same body yet feel quite different, so it pays to notice both how heavy a wine is and how smooth it feels.

Alcohol makes wine slightly more viscous than water, meaning thicker and slower to flow, and it adds a gentle warmth. In an Australian trial with Riesling, raising the alcohol made two of the three wines feel fuller. Glycerol, a smooth, slightly sweet substance that yeast makes while turning sugar into alcohol, is often given credit for body too. But studies disagree on how much it matters at the levels found in dry wine. Alcohol and extract remain the safe answer.

Experts measure extract in grams per litre: what is left after drying out a sample completely. Most wines have roughly 17 to 30 grams per litre, and reds usually have more than whites. That is thanks to the colour and tannin, the drying feel many reds have, that come from their skins. A related figure, sugar-free extract, leaves the sugar out, so it shows the grapes' substance apart from any sweetness.

Climate is not the only lever: ripeness also depends on when the grower picks. Pinot Grigio is the Italian name for Pinot Gris. In Italy it is usually picked early for a light, crisp style, while in Alsace, in eastern France, the same grape often makes much fuller wines. So the grape's name tells you less about body than you might think. The place, and the style the winemaker chose, tell you more.

Body is easiest to judge by comparison. Water makes a handy baseline: sip some, then sip the wine, and notice how much more weight the wine has. Tasting two wines side by side helps even more. High alcohol often shows as a gentle warmth at the back of your throat, a hint that the wine will feel fuller. Remember that body and sweetness are separate: a completely dry wine can still feel rich.

Basic Beaujolais is made from Gamay, a grape that gives juicy reds low in tannin, the drying feel many reds have, and it is often served lightly chilled. Chianti, made mainly from Sangiovese, is a classic medium-bodied red. Cabernet Sauvignon is a thick-skinned grape, and those skins give plenty of colour and tannin, which is part of its extract and its weight.

deeper.body: Swirling leaves a thin film of wine on the glass. Alcohol evaporates from it faster than water, so the film becomes more watery. Water has a higher surface tension than alcohol, meaning its surface pulls together more strongly. So the watery film pulls more wine up from the bowl below. The wine gathers into a ridge, grows heavy and falls back as tears. Scientists call this the Marangoni effect.
deeper.title: Why the tears climb the glass

deeper.key: Alcohol evaporates from the film, the film becomes more watery, and its higher surface tension pulls wine up.
opts: Sugar left in the film turns thick and sticky
It has lost alcohol, so surface tension rises
The warm glass draws the wine upwards
Bubbles of trapped gas push the wine up
deeper.q: Why does the film of wine on the glass pull more wine upwards?
deeper.remember: Less alcohol in the film, more pull on the wine.
deeper.why: Because alcohol drives the whole process, tears are a clue to how strong, and so how full, a wine is.

deeper.body: After fermentation, dead yeast cells called lees settle at the bottom of the tank or barrel. Leaving a wine on them for months, and sometimes stirring them up, a step called bâtonnage, gives a rounder, creamier texture. Time in oak barrels can round a wine out too. Together they help explain why an oaked Chardonnay feels so much bigger than a crisp, unoaked white.
deeper.title: Lees and oak add cream

deeper.key: Stirring the lees, called bâtonnage, gives a wine a rounder, creamier, fuller texture.
deeper.q: Winemakers stir the lees to make a wine feel thinner and lighter.
deeper.remember: Stir the lees, add the cream.
deeper.why: It is one reason an oaked, lees-aged Chardonnay feels so much bigger than a crisp, unoaked white.

deeper.body: Body is one of the most useful clues when pairing wine with food. A light wine suits delicate dishes, like a leafy salad or white fish. A full wine stands up to rich ones, like a beef stew. Get it wrong and one side wins: a big red can swamp a delicate dish, and a light wine can taste thin and watery next to heavy food.
deeper.title: Match weight with weight

deeper.key: Light wines go with delicate food and full wines with rich food.
opts: Light Pinot Grigio with delicate white fish
Full Cabernet Sauvignon with a rich beef stew
Full oaked Chardonnay with a plain leafy salad
Light Beaujolais with a heavy, slow-cooked stew
deeper.q: Which of these pairings match weight with weight?
deeper.remember: Light with light, rich with rich.
deeper.why: Matched weights let both the wine and the dish show; a mismatch lets one side swamp the other.
